title: The Goophered Grapevine
focus: a story told to protect a livelihood

teacherSummary.text: A white Northerner, John, considers buying a run-down North Carolina vineyard. Julius McAdoo, a formerly enslaved man, tells him it is 'goophered' (conjured): before the war, an enslaved man named Henry ate its grapes, and his life rose and fell with the vines until he died. John buys anyway and later suspects Julius told the tale because he profited from the grapes; he hires Julius as coachman.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “goophered” slowly and put it in my own words: Julius tells the Northern newcomer that the grapevines are bewitched by a conjure spell. Next, craft. I notice the word is dialect from African American folk belief, set inside the narrator's polished standard English. The strongest word is “goophered”: the whole story turns on this one unfamiliar word, which the outsider has to have explained. Then, effect. What does Julius mean when he says the vineyard is "goophered"? My answer: Julius uses the conjure tale to make the vineyard seem dangerous, partly to protect the grapes he has been enjoying; the word shows he is cleverer than the narrator thinks.

segments.script: Annotate the story for framenarrative, irony (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this story suggest about a story told to protect a livelihood? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how The Goophered Grapevine develops the idea of a story told to protect a livelihood. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and diction / vocabulary shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Julius's tale is both entertainment and an act of resistance. When the text says “Mars Dugal' up 'n tuk Henry ter town, en sole 'im fer fifteen hunder' dollars” (The Goophered Grapevine, paragraph 40), it shows this directly. The "goophered" vines protect his own income, and the detail that the master "sole 'im fer fifteen hunder' dollars" when Henry was strong exposes an economy that treated a man like a crop.
